reviews.text:
My account was flagged because its display name was "Metal Tesla." The name comes from my personal license plate (METAL) and my Tesla Model Y. I'm not impersonating anyone, and I tried to fix it right away.
The name change page X showed me was broken. Every name I entered gave an error, including my real name and "Fan" or "Parody" labels. I opened a support ticket on Oct 27 and never got a real answer. Then the account was moved to permanent read-only, and the name change page disappeared completely.
Since then I've filed multiple appeals through the official form. Each one is denied by an automated email within about a minute. The emails say I broke a rule but leave the "specifically" field blank, and they tell me to log in and follow on-screen instructions that don't exist. Resubmitting just says my case is "already in the queue."
I even contacted xAI support. They told me they can't see my X ticket or change anything on X and sent me back to X. So nobody can help.
I'm a paying Premium subscriber and I'm willing to change my name, bio, photo, or add any label X requires. I just need a screen that works or one human to look at the account. Until then, the app gives you no way out of a broken process. One star as support is nonexistent. I will change this rating to five stars if I ever get a fix. It’s been over two weeks.

reviews.title: Free speech shouldn’t need a VIP pass
reviews.text:
I was permanently banned from Twitter after posting a scathing critique and satire of Klaus Schwab and the World Economic Forum. From my perspective, it was censorship - not a credible response to political commentary.

Satire is supposed to make powerful people uncomfortable. If it must first pass the comfort test of those it mocks, it becomes public relations.

I accept that platforms need rules. Threats and harassment are not debate. But sharp criticism of influential public figures and institutions deserves a clear distinction and permanent bans deserve transparent explanations and meaningful appeals.

Twitter (X) sells itself as the digital town square. 

My experience felt more like a privately managed shopping centre: speak freely, provided you don’t upset management.

Apply the rules consistently. Explain the decisions. Let people challenge them.

A platform’s commitment to free speech is tested by the criticism it tolerates and not the slogans it markets.

reviews.title: Digital sewer
reviews.text:
X feels less like a social platform and more like a digital sewer. The feed is a constant stream of rage bait, misinformation, and obvious bot activity, all seemingly boosted rather than controlled. Meaningful conversation is drowned out by the loudest, angriest, and most divisive content, creating an environment that feels intentionally engineered to provoke outrage instead of understanding.

Misinformation spreads unchecked, often going viral before any context or correction has a chance to catch up—if it ever does. Bots and bad-faith actors are everywhere, amplifying extreme takes and turning every topic, no matter how trivial, into a culture war. The result is a platform that feels hostile, exhausting, and toxic to engage with for more than a few minutes at a time.

What’s most frustrating is that X could be useful. There are still smart people, journalists, artists, and experts trying to share real insight—but they’re buried under piles of spam, propaganda, and performative outrage. The algorithm doesn’t reward nuance or honesty; it rewards whatever makes people the angriest the fastest.

At this point, using X feels like willingly jumping into a pit of noise and negativity. Instead of informing or connecting people, it divides them, monetizes their anger, and leaves the overall discourse worse than it found it. If this is the future of the platform, it’s hard to see why anyone interested in reality, good-faith discussion, or mental well-being would want to stay.
